column5: name exalted above earth and heaven
column6: The commentary joins “exalt the Lord’s name” to al-aʿla; this psalm says the Lord’s name alone is exalted and his majesty is above earth and heaven, an unusually close praise formula.

column5: call on and proclaim the exalted name
column6: The commentary’s command to praise the high name is matched by Isaiah’s thanksgiving instruction to call on the Lord’s name and proclaim among the nations that it is exalted.

column5: Hebrew ʿelyon and Arabic al-aʿla
column6: The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with the elevation root ʿ-l-w; here YHWH is called ʿelyon, “Most High,” over all the earth, a related Semitic elevation title in a declaration of divine supremacy.

column5: Hebrew ʿelyon and Arabic al-aʿla
column6: The commentary’s “Most High” language has a Hebrew counterpart in Melchizedek’s blessing of God as ʿelyon; the verse blesses that God for delivering Abram’s enemies, joining the title to praise and sovereignty.

column5: Most High with the lowly
column6: The commentary sets the Lord’s highness against the low, near life and a ruler’s vaunted height; Isaiah calls God the High and Lofty One who also dwells with the contrite and lowly, redefining true elevation.

column5: majestic name and glory above the heavens
column6: The commentary says the named one is lifted by the name; this prayer calls YHWH’s name majestic throughout the earth and places his glory above the heavens.

column5: Lord high above nations
column6: The commentary contrasts the truly exalted Lord with a creature claiming the highest rank; this hymn places YHWH above all nations and his glory above the heavens.

column5: enthroned on high
column6: The commentary’s al-aʿla denotes real divine elevation, unlike Pharaoh’s self-assertion; this praise asks who is like the Lord, enthroned on high.

column5: praise and exaltation after deliverance
column6: The commentary’s command to glorify the Lord’s name is matched by Moses’ song, which calls the Lord “my God” and says he will praise and exalt him after the sea deliverance.

column5: exaltation and praise of the name
column6: The commentary links tasbih with raising the Lord’s name; Isaiah says “I will exalt you” and praise the Lord’s name for faithful wonders, giving that pairing a worship context.

column5: great and holy name praised
column6: The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of every fault; this psalm calls for praise of the Lord’s great, awesome name and declares him holy.

column5: Hebrew z-k-r: remembering the name
column6: The commentary’s ذَكَرَ is “remembered/mentioned”; the psalmist says he remembered the Lord’s name at night and kept the law, a direct Hebrew cognate in a devotional setting.

column5: name and memorial through generations
column6: The commentary links remembrance to the Lord’s name; God identifies himself to Moses and says this name is his memorial through all generations, using the Hebrew z-k-r family for enduring remembrance.

column5: remembering the Lord’s name against worldly reliance
column6: The commentary’s remembered name marks the worshipper’s orientation toward the Lord; this verse contrasts those who trust chariots and horses with those who remember the name of YHWH their God.

column5: remembrance and reverence for the name
column6: The commentary’s dhikr links remembrance with the Lord’s honor; Malachi says those who fear the Lord and esteem his name speak together, and a book of remembrance is written for them.

column5: remembered royal name and enduring praise
column6: The commentary says naming raises the named one’s remembrance; in this royal wedding poem the speaker promises the king’s name will be remembered through generations and peoples will praise him, though the addressee is the king, not explicitly YHWH.

column5: house and the Lord’s name
column6: The commentary cites houses raised for worship where the Lord’s name is mentioned; Solomon calls the temple the place where God said his name would be, tying a worship house to the indwelling name.

column5: a tower reaching heaven and a self-made name
column6: The commentary contrasts the Lord’s high name with a ruler’s false elevation; Babel’s builders seek a name for themselves while building a tower toward heaven, joining self-exaltation and name-making in one scene.

column5: failed ascent and scattering
column6: The commentary’s high/low axis includes a creature’s attempt to rise; after Babel’s tower project, God scatters the builders and the city is left unfinished, a narrative reversal of their ascent and self-made name.

column5: “I will make myself like the Most High”
column6: The commentary cites Pharaoh claiming “I am your Lord Most High”; the taunting king in Isaiah explicitly resolves to make himself like the Most High, exposing the same creaturely seizure of divine height.

column5: cast down from claimed height
column6: The commentary says a king’s rising can mean tyranny and arrogance; Isaiah’s self-exalting figure is brought down to Sheol, supplying the reversal implicit in the Qur’anic judgment on Pharaoh.

column5: prince claims divine status
column6: The commentary’s Pharaoh appropriates the Lord’s highest title; Ezekiel addresses Tyre’s ruler as a man who says “I am a god” while sitting in a godlike seat, another ruler’s false claim to divine rank.

column5: king boasts of his own majesty
column6: The commentary identifies Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as arrogant self-exaltation; Nebuchadnezzar claims Babylon was built by his own power for the glory of his majesty, making the ruler’s boast explicit.

column5: Aramaic title for the Most High
column6: The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with an elevation root; after his humiliation Nebuchadnezzar blesses the Aramaic “Most High” and praises his everlasting dominion, coupling a related Semitic title with worship.

column5: pride humbled, heavenly king praised
column6: The commentary opposes God’s true highness to a creature’s arrogance; Nebuchadnezzar honors the King of heaven and concludes that those who walk in pride God is able to humble.

column5: human pride lowered, Lord alone exalted
column6: The commentary makes height reversible when a ruler exalts himself; Isaiah says the proud eyes of humanity will be brought low and YHWH alone exalted.

column5: Pharaoh asks who YHWH is
column6: The commentary quotes Pharaoh’s direct claim to be the highest lord; Exodus instead has Pharaoh deny knowing YHWH and refuse obedience, preserving a distinct biblical portrayal of the same ruler’s resistance.

column5: Pharaoh’s survival serves God’s name
column6: The commentary’s Pharaoh claims the highest rank for himself; God tells the biblical Pharaoh he has been kept standing so divine power may be shown and God’s name proclaimed throughout the earth, reversing the claim.

column5: magicians recognize God’s act but are not converted
column6: The commentary notes that Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Exodus has Pharaoh’s magicians admit “the finger of God” but remain in the confrontation, without the conversion and reward narrated in the Qur’anic scene.

column5: holiness and incomparable majesty
column6: The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of evil and cites divine majesty; Moses’ song asks who is like the Lord, majestic in holiness and awesome in deeds.

column5: claiming power for oneself
column6: The commentary treats Pharaoh’s self-ascribed height as arrogance; Moses warns Israel against saying “my power and the might of my hand” made its wealth, a specific warning against taking divine provision as one’s own greatness.

column5: worship under threat of the furnace
column6: The commentary joins praise of the Lord’s high name to the great fire; after the three Judeans survive Nebuchadnezzar’s blazing furnace, the king blesses their God because they refused to worship any god but him.

column5: fire of judgment
column6: The commentary names the great fire awaiting the wretched; Isaiah’s closing vision shows the corpses of rebels with an unquenched fire, a related scriptural image of divine judgment by fire.

column5: Aramaic š-b-ḥ, praise in prayer
column6: The commentary labels سَبِّحِ as tasbih, glorifying God; Daniel thanks and praises the God of his fathers for revealing the king’s secret, using the Aramaic praise cognate in a prayer that credits divine wisdom.

column5: this world as a vestibule to the world to come
column6: The commentary hears al-dunya as the lower and nearer life that people choose; Avot calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation for entry into the latter.

column5: relative worth of the two worlds
column6: The commentary’s choice of the nearer life is a value judgment; Avot says one hour of good deeds in this world is better than the whole world to come, yet one hour of serenity in the world to come is better than all this world, preserving both sides of the contrast.

column5: magnifying and sanctifying the great name
column6: The commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; the Qaddish opens with a prayer that God’s great name be magnified and sanctified in the world he created.

column5: Babel’s tower as rebellion against God
column6: The commentary treats a creature’s claim to height as arrogant usurpation; Genesis Rabbah reads the tower builders’ ascent as rebellion against heaven, making the biblical tower more than an architectural project.

column5: worship and glorification of the Lord of Spirits’ name
column6: The commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise and highness; 1 Enoch pictures earth’s inhabitants falling down to worship and bless, glorify, and celebrate the name of the Lord of Spirits.

column5: prayer that the Father’s name be hallowed
column6: The commentary’s opening command is praise of the Lord’s name; Jesus’ prayer begins by asking that the Father’s name be hallowed, placing sanctification of the name inside communal prayer.

column5: “My soul magnifies the Lord”
column6: The commentary links the Lord’s name and remembered honor to elevation; Mary’s prayer begins by magnifying the Lord, a direct worship formula from a lowly speaker.

column5: holiness of the name
column6: The commentary’s tasbih declares God free of defect and exalts his name; Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her and holy is his name.

column5: mighty brought down, lowly exalted
column6: The commentary pairs a self-exalting ruler with the low/near life; Mary’s hymn says God brings rulers down from thrones and exalts the lowly, a direct reversal of claimed human height.

column5: “Father, glorify your name”
column6: The commentary’s command to raise the Lord’s name is echoed when Jesus prays that the Father glorify his name; the heavenly voice answers that it has been glorified and will be glorified again.

column5: exalted and given the name above every name
column6: The commentary says the Lord’s name is raised and honored; Paul says God highly exalted Jesus and bestowed the name above every name, locating exaltation in the Christ hymn.

column5: every knee bows at the name
column6: The commentary’s name-and-prayer pairing becomes embodied worship here: at Jesus’ name every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is to bow.

column5: confession to God’s glory
column6: The commentary joins remembering the Lord’s name to prayer; Paul says every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord to the glory of God the Father.

column5: praise and confession of the name
column6: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord’s name before prayer; Hebrews describes continual praise as a sacrifice of lips that confess God’s name.

column5: nations glorify the holy name
column6: The commentary links tasbih, majesty, and the Lord’s name; Revelation asks who will not fear and glorify God’s name, then says he alone is holy and nations will worship.

column5: thanksgiving for the holy name in prayer
column6: The commentary’s remembered and praised name is a liturgical act; the post-meal prayer thanks the holy Father for his holy name made to dwell in believers’ hearts.

column5: self-exaltation reversed
column6: The commentary calls Pharaoh’s highest-lord claim arrogance; Jesus says the one who exalts himself will be humbled and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.

column5: humility before the Lord brings exaltation
column6: The commentary makes height and lowliness an axis; James commands readers to humble themselves before the Lord, who will exalt them.

column5: humility under God’s mighty hand
column6: The commentary contrasts the proud ruler with the lowly life; Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God’s mighty hand so he may exalt them at the proper time.

column5: Moses refuses temporary pleasure
column6: The commentary places Moses’ story beside the warning against choosing the near life; Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God’s people over the temporary pleasure of sin.

column5: Moses values reward above Egypt’s wealth
column6: The commentary’s low-life choice is a question of value; Hebrews says Moses considered reproach greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures because he looked to the reward.

column5: the world passes, God’s will abides
column6: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life; John contrasts the passing world and its desires with the one who does God’s will and abides forever.

column5: gaining the world and losing one’s life
column6: The commentary criticizes preferring the low, near life; Jesus asks what it profits someone to gain the whole world and forfeit life, making the choice’s cost explicit.

column5: Jannes and Jambres oppose Moses
column6: The commentary says Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Paul names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses who resist the truth, preserving a contrary Christian memory of the magicians.

column5: unapproachable light and eternal honor
column6: The commentary links divine majesty and light with the great fire; Paul describes God as dwelling in unapproachable light and as the one to whom honor and eternal dominion belong.

column5: eternal fire of judgment
column6: The commentary names the great fire as the wretched person’s end; Jesus’ judgment scene sends the accursed into eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

column5: treasure on earth decays
column6: The commentary says people prefer the near, lower life; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy, giving the choice a concrete object and cost.

column5: treasure in heaven endures
column6: Against the commentary’s preference for the near life, Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven, where it cannot be destroyed, supplying the alternative value.

column5: exalt the Lord’s name together
column6: The commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; in David’s psalm the worshippers are told to magnify YHWH together and exalt his name together, a direct communal formulation.

column5: name praised from sunrise to sunset
column6: The commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise; this hymn says the Lord’s name is to be praised from the rising of the sun to its setting, extending the act across the whole day.

column5: glory due the name and offerings in the courts
column6: The commentary links raised houses, the Lord’s name, and worship; the psalm tells worshippers to ascribe glory to the Lord’s name and bring an offering into his courts.

column5: chosen sanctuary where God places his name
column6: The commentary cites houses authorized for worship with the Lord’s name in them; Deuteronomy commands Israel to seek the place God chooses for his name and dwelling, supplying the covenant sanctuary background.

column5: altar and remembered name
column6: The commentary links remembering the Lord’s name with prayer; God says he will come and bless at every altar where he causes his name to be remembered, joining invocation to sacrifice.

column5: great name among nations and pure offering
column6: The commentary ties praise of the Lord’s name to worship in houses; Malachi says the Lord’s name is great among the nations and that offerings are made to it across the earth.

column5: glorious name exalted above blessing and praise
column6: The commentary commands exaltation of the Lord’s name; the Levites’ public prayer blesses God’s glorious name, exalted above all blessing and praise.

column5: blessed name in bereavement
column6: The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of every evil; after losing his children and possessions Job blesses the Lord’s name, showing praise under calamity rather than only in prosperity.

column5: blessed name, kings raised and removed
column6: The commentary contrasts God’s true height with a ruler’s claim; Daniel blesses God’s name forever because wisdom and might belong to him and he removes and sets up kings.

column5: Most High rules human kingdoms
column6: The commentary’s Pharaoh claims supreme rule for himself; the heavenly decree in Daniel says the Most High rules the kingdom of humanity and gives it to whom he wills, framing Nebuchadnezzar’s later boast and humbling.

column5: kingdom taken during the king’s boast
column6: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “I am the highest lord” as a creature’s false claim; Daniel’s heavenly voice interrupts Nebuchadnezzar’s boast and announces that his kingship has departed from him.

column5: the Lord descends and proclaims his name
column6: The commentary calls for praise of the Lord’s name; at Sinai the Lord descends in a cloud and proclaims the divine name before Moses, giving the naming formula a theophanic setting.

column5: name proclaimed through merciful attributes
column6: The commentary defines tasbih as denying every evil of God; the proclamation following the name calls the Lord merciful, gracious, patient, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.

column5: light of the Lord’s face
column6: The commentary’s cited expression about the radiance, majesty, and light of the Lord’s face has a close benediction parallel: the priest asks that the Lord make his face shine upon Israel.

column5: prayer for the light of God’s face
column6: The commentary connects the Lord’s face with glory and light; the psalmist prays for the light of God’s face to shine upon the worshippers, making the image explicitly devotional.

column5: seeing God’s face and the limit of mortal life
column6: The commentary cites language about the Lord’s face as overwhelming glory and light; when Moses asks to see God’s glory, Exodus says no human can see God’s face and live, setting a distinct boundary around that face imagery.

column5: glory appearing as devouring fire on the mountain
column6: The commentary connects divine majesty and light with the great fire; at Sinai the Lord’s glory appears to Israel like a devouring fire on the mountain’s summit, joining height, glory, and fire.

column5: the Lord as consuming fire
column6: The commentary names the great fire in the judgment scene; Moses warns Israel that the Lord their God is a consuming fire, so the fire image also expresses divine holiness and judgment.

column5: Hannah’s exaltation and praise
column6: The commentary pairs the Lord’s exaltation with a worshipper’s prayer; Hannah says her strength is exalted in the Lord and rejoices in his salvation, placing elevation in grateful devotion rather than self-claim.

column5: God brings low and raises up
column6: The commentary makes highness and lowliness opposite ends of one axis; Hannah’s prayer says the Lord makes poor and rich and brings low and raises up.

column5: the needy raised from dust to sit with princes
column6: The commentary describes the chosen life as low and lesser; Hannah says God lifts the needy from the dust and seats them with princes, a concrete reversal of low status.

column5: God raises the humble and casts down the wicked
column6: The commentary contrasts true divine elevation with a ruler’s arrogance; the psalm says the Lord raises the humble and casts the wicked down, assigning the upward and downward movement to God.

column5: God puts one down and lifts another
column6: The commentary treats elevation as the Lord’s rightful attribute and worldly self-exaltation as false; the psalm calls God the judge who brings one down and raises another.

column5: Hebrew kabbir and Arabic k-b-r
column6: The commentary labels ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ with k-b-r and explains tekbir as declaring God great; Job calls God kabbir, “mighty,” attesting a related Semitic greatness word, though the Hebrew verse emphasizes might.

column5: one king over earth and one name
column6: The commentary praises the Lord as highest and links the name to worship; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and his name one, uniting universal rule with the divine name.

column5: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in the self-made name
column6: The commentary labels ٱسْمَ as a name whose mention is raised; Babel’s builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower toward heaven. Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, though the Hebrew verse does not derive it from height.

column5: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in praise
column6: The commentary labels ٱسْمَ as the name that raises the named one’s remembrance; the psalm calls YHWH’s shem majestic throughout the earth. The cognate appears in a praise formula, without importing the commentary’s proposed etymology.

column5: morning star fallen from heaven
column6: The commentary develops a silhouette rising above the horizon and a ruler’s claimed height; Isaiah addresses a fallen morning star before recounting the speaker’s ascent and boast, adding a celestial image to the self-exaltation scene.

column5: throne glory, streams of fire, and unapproachable face
column6: The commentary’s gloss connects the Lord’s facial radiance and majesty with light and fire; Enoch’s heavenly throne vision joins fiery streams to overwhelming glory and a face no flesh can behold.

column5: God scatters the proud
column6: The commentary treats Pharaoh’s claim to highest rank as arrogance; Mary’s hymn says God scatters the proud in the intention of their hearts, adding the divine reversal of self-exaltation.

column5: treasure reveals the heart’s allegiance
column6: The commentary says people choose the low and near life; Jesus says the heart follows its treasure, making the preference for earthly life an inward allegiance rather than a mere circumstance.

column5: choice between God and wealth
column6: The commentary names a choice of the lower, nearer life; Jesus says no one can serve both God and mammon, making that preference a direct choice of master.

column5: Paul reads Pharaoh’s role as serving God’s name
column6: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as false human elevation; Paul quotes Exodus to say Pharaoh was raised up so God’s power and name would be proclaimed, interpreting the same ruler as an instrument of divine sovereignty.

column5: God’s glory shines in Christ’s face
column6: The commentary’s gloss joins radiance and light to the Lord’s face; Paul describes the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ, with light shining in human hearts.

column5: visible transient things and unseen eternal things
column6: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life and the surah contrasts it with what lasts; Paul says visible things are temporary while unseen things are eternal.

column5: trying to save life and losing it
column6: The commentary warns that people prefer the low, near life; Jesus says whoever seeks to save life will lose it, while whoever loses life for his sake will save it.

column5: set the mind above, not on earth
column6: The commentary sets the high against the near earthly life; Paul commands believers to seek the things above rather than things on earth, stating that orientation directly.

column5: earthly-mindedness as the road to destruction
column6: The commentary calls the chosen earthly life low and nearer; Paul describes people whose minds are set on earthly things and whose end is destruction, supplying a concrete moral consequence.

column5: citizenship in heaven
column6: The commentary’s axis contrasts the near life with a higher enduring orientation; Paul says believers’ citizenship is in heaven, naming the alternative to earthly-mindedness.

column5: God as consuming fire in a call to worship
column6: The commentary links divine majesty and the great fire; Hebrews urges reverent worship because God is a consuming fire, bringing the image into a Christian liturgical warning.

column5: Satan falls from heaven
column6: The commentary sets true divine height against a creature’s arrogant claim; Jesus says he saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning, a specific heavenly fall that resonates with the descent of Isaiah’s self-exalting figure.

column5: Mary’s “magnifying” as the soul’s reception of God
column6: The commentary says the name raises the named one’s remembrance; Origen’s homily on Mary’s Magnificat explains her soul’s magnifying of the Lord as a change in the human recipient’s capacity to perceive and receive God, not an increase in God’s greatness.
